vignette:
Alyssa, a 25-year-old North American woman working as a bus driver, came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed to a moving watchtower. The traumatic event she kept returning to was a military incident overseas, when a routine stretch of duty became suddenly chaotic and unpredictable. She described the moment as one in which everything went wrong at once: the atmosphere shifted, her body went sharply on alert, and the sense that she had any control vanished. Since then, she has found that ordinary stress can carry the same charge as those moments in service. On crowded routes, when traffic backs up unexpectedly or a rider starts arguing at the farebox, she feels her attention snap outward and she begins constantly scanning her surroundings for signs of danger, as if she has to catch the threat before it catches her. Those reminders do not just unsettle her; they immediately make the bus, the depot, and the streets around her feel dangerous, as though the next argument or sudden movement could turn into the same emergency she lived through overseas. The same happens when she notices herself getting dizzy or lightheaded after a long shift; that somatic feeling is enough to pull her back into the sense that something is about to happen, and her body responds with strong physical reactions that feel out of proportion even to her. Once the reminder has taken hold, she is left with the thought that she must be damaged and no longer capable of doing her job safely, a conclusion that has made her feel that her life has been changed in ways she cannot undo.

Over time, Alyssa had come to believe that the trauma had taken more than her sense of safety. She said plainly that her life had been destroyed by it, and that nothing in it felt meaningful anymore. That belief has made her hyperaware of anything that might signal danger, so even ordinary things she once would have ignored — a passenger’s raised voice, the glare of headlights at dusk, a sudden shift in traffic — now stand out as warning signs that seem to prove the world is unsafe. Before the incident, being a bus driver had felt connected to the disciplined, capable part of herself she recognized from military service; now she spoke about the job as evidence that she is no longer capable of doing the things that defined her. That belief has shaped the way she moves through the world. A day that used to feel ordinary now feels full of pressure points: a route with a sudden detour, a passenger boarding in an agitated mood, even the shift from daylight to dusk can make her think she cannot trust herself to manage what comes next. Those thoughts do not stay contained. They feed her sense of danger, and as she scans every mirror, every sidewalk, every movement at the curb, the bus cabin itself becomes another place where she feels she must know exactly where the exits are and keep her back against a wall or bulkhead whenever she steps off the vehicle, so she can see the room and avoid being caught off guard.

What frightened Alyssa most was how quickly the body alarm could be set off by reminders she never expected. A feeling of dizziness at the end of a double shift, the stress of running late, or the unpredictability of a crowded station can all bring back the same jolt of physical arousal she felt during the military event. That constant sense of danger has quietly confirmed her worst fears about herself, leaving her more certain that she is not who she was before and that something fundamental in her has been broken by what happened. She notices the surge immediately and then assumes it means she is failing again, which deepens her conviction that she is no longer capable and that her life has been ruined. Those appraisals, in turn, make the world seem even more dangerous, so she scans harder, watches people’s hands and eyes, and positions herself where she can see the whole room. The more she watches for danger, the more every unexpected noise, conflict, or change in routine feels like proof that she was right to stay on guard, and each one becomes another reminder of the trauma. In the depot, she now avoids chatting with coworkers in the break room because she cannot tolerate sitting with her back to an open space; on the route, she prefers the same seat angle, the same mirror checks, the same careful habits, all in an effort to keep the panic from rising.

As the weeks and months passed, this pattern began to consume the life Alyssa once organized around competence and service. She still shows up for work, but she does so with a vigilance that leaves her exhausted and detached, and she has increasingly withdrawn from friends because she cannot find words for why everything feels so empty. She sought help at last after a near-miss on her route left her shaking and convinced she would either lose control of the bus or miss something dangerous at the roadside. What she is most afraid of now is not only being harmed, but becoming so overwhelmed by fear that she can no longer do the work that once defined her. What she is hoping for, though she says it carefully, is to feel like herself again long enough to believe that her future is not already gone.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows reminders leading to threat, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers themselves drive or cause a sense of threat in the required causal way.
The vignette includes reminders and negative beliefs, but no paragraph clearly says that triggers lead to those negative appraisals.
The vignette shows negative appraisals and later mentions reminders, but it does not explicitly convey that the negative beliefs cause the triggers or reminders.
The vignette shows threat and negative beliefs, but no paragraph clearly states that feeling threatened leads to the negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette shows reminders leading to threat, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers themselves drive or cause a sense of threat in the required causal way.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette includes reminders and negative beliefs, but no paragraph clearly says that triggers lead to those negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows negative appraisals and later mentions reminders, but it does not explicitly convey that the negative beliefs cause the triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat and negative beliefs, but no paragraph clearly states that feeling threatened leads to the negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
